title: Quorum
text: A quorum is the minimum number of replicas that must take part in an operation for it to count as successful, usually a strict majority. Because any two majorities overlap in at least one member, quorum-based reads and writes can guarantee that a read sees the most recent acknowledged write. In leaderless stores this is expressed as R + W > N.

title: Linearizability
text: Linearizability is a consistency model in which every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and its completion. The system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data, so once a write is acknowledged, every later read observes it. It is the strongest single-object guarantee and the meaning of C in the CAP theorem.

title: Idempotency
text: An operation is idempotent when applying it several times produces the same result as applying it once. Idempotent handlers make retries safe after ambiguous failures such as timeouts. APIs commonly achieve this with client-supplied idempotency keys that let the server detect and deduplicate repeated requests.

title: Tombstone
text: A tombstone is a marker written to record that a key or element was deleted, rather than physically removing it right away. It lets the deletion propagate to other replicas and shadow older copies of the value. Tombstones are purged later by compaction or garbage collection once every replica is known to have seen them.

title: Compaction
text: Compaction is a background process that merges data files, drops overwritten values and expired deletion markers, and rewrites the survivors into fewer, larger files. It is central to log-structured storage engines, where it bounds read cost and reclaims disk space. Its scheduling strongly influences write amplification and latency spikes.

title: Fencing Token
text: A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued each time a lock or lease is granted. The protected resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects requests carrying an older one. This prevents a client that paused and lost its lease from corrupting data after a newer holder has taken over.

title: Split-Brain
text: Split-brain is a failure where a network partition or failed failover leaves two nodes each believing it is the primary. Both accept writes, and their histories diverge in ways that may be impossible to merge cleanly. Majority quorums, fencing, and leases are the usual defenses.

title: Heartbeat
text: A heartbeat is a small periodic message a process sends to show that it is still alive. Peers or a coordinator that miss several consecutive heartbeats suspect the sender has failed and may trigger failover or an election. Choosing the interval and timeout balances detection speed against false alarms during brief network hiccups.

title: Replication Lag
text: Replication lag is the delay between a write being applied on the primary and that same write becoming visible on a replica. During the lag, reads from the replica return stale data, which can confuse users who just made a change. It is usually measured in seconds or in bytes of log not yet applied.

title: Sharding
text: Sharding splits a dataset horizontally into partitions, called shards, that live on different machines. Each record is assigned to a shard by a key using ranges or hashing, so storage and throughput scale by adding nodes. Cross-shard queries and transactions become more expensive and rebalancing must be planned carefully.

title: Write Amplification
text: Write amplification is the ratio of bytes physically written to storage versus bytes logically written by the application. Compaction, page rewrites, journaling, and flash translation layers all inflate it. High amplification wears out SSDs faster and consumes bandwidth that could serve user traffic.

title: Tail Latency
text: Tail latency refers to the slowest responses in a latency distribution, typically measured at the 99th or 99.9th percentile. When a single request fans out to many backends, the slowest one determines overall response time, so rare stragglers become common for users. Hedged requests, timeouts, and reducing pause-inducing work help tame the tail.

title: Backpressure
text: Backpressure is a feedback mechanism by which an overloaded consumer signals producers to slow down instead of silently buffering unbounded work. It can take the form of bounded queues that block, flow-control windows, or explicit rejections. Without it, memory grows until the system crashes or latency becomes unacceptable.

title: Eventual Consistency
text: Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. It allows replicas to accept reads and writes independently, favoring availability and low latency. In the meantime, clients may observe stale or temporarily conflicting data.

title: Snapshot Isolation
text: Snapshot isolation is a transaction isolation level in which each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database taken at its start. Concurrent writes to the same row conflict, and one of the transactions is aborted. It prevents most read anomalies but still permits write skew.

title: Leader Election
text: Leader election is the process by which nodes in a cluster choose a single coordinator responsible for ordering writes or assigning work. Elections typically run after the current leader stops sending heartbeats and require votes from a majority. Correct protocols ensure at most one leader is recognized per term or epoch.

title: Hinted Handoff
text: Hinted handoff lets a healthy node temporarily accept a write intended for an unreachable replica and store it with a hint naming the real owner. When the owner comes back online, the stored writes are forwarded to it. This keeps writes available during short outages but is not a substitute for full repair.

title: Anti-Entropy
text: Anti-entropy is a background repair process in which replicas compare their data and fix any differences. Comparisons are made efficient by exchanging digests such as Merkle tree hashes, so only divergent ranges are transferred. It catches inconsistencies that read repair and hinted handoff miss.

title: Consistent Snapshot
text: A consistent snapshot is a captured global state of a distributed system that could have occurred in some valid execution, meaning no message is recorded as received without also being recorded as sent. Algorithms such as Chandy-Lamport take one without stopping the system by circulating marker messages. Such snapshots are used for checkpointing, backups, and debugging.

title: At-Least-Once Delivery
text: At-least-once delivery is a messaging guarantee that every message will be delivered one or more times, never zero. Senders achieve it by retrying until they receive an acknowledgment, which means duplicates are possible after lost acks. Consumers therefore need idempotent processing or deduplication to avoid double effects.
